headline: A Thirsty Coyote Turns an LA Salon Skylight Into a Watering Hole
lede: A Los Angeles hairdresser named Travis Ogletree got an unusual view in late April 2025: a coyote perched on his salon roof, lapping rainwater pooled on the skylight glass directly above his head. The footage, captured on camera and shared widely, became a minor viral moment. It is also a small, vivid document of how thoroughly coyotes have settled into American urban life.
body:
The clip is straightforward: a coyote crouches on a skylight, tongue working steadily at standing water, apparently unbothered by the humans visible beneath the glass. What makes it arresting is the geometry — the animal seen from below, a wild predator framed like a ceiling fixture. Ogletree, who owns the salon, reportedly laughed it off rather than called animal control.

Coyotes (*Canis latrans*) have expanded their range dramatically over the past century, moving from the western plains into every major American city, including Chicago, New York, and Los Angeles. They thrive in fragmented urban landscapes by eating almost anything — rodents, fruit, pet food left outside, and, apparently, skylight runoff. Los Angeles, with its sprawling hillside neighborhoods abutting open chaparral, is one of the densest urban coyote habitats in the country.

The behavior on display — scaling a commercial roof in search of water — is consistent with what wildlife researchers call **opportunistic foraging**: coyotes learn quickly which human structures offer resources and return to them. A rooftop skylight retaining rainwater is, from the animal's perspective, a reliable puddle in an otherwise impermeable cityscape.

The footage circulated through ABC News and AccuWeather among other outlets, slotted into the light-news category of charming animal encounters. But it carries a subtler edge: the coyote is not lost or confused. It is at home. The salon, from its vantage, is just terrain.

concepts.definition: Over the twentieth century, coyotes colonized nearly every North American city, exploiting the same adaptability that let them survive western predator-control campaigns. They navigate traffic, exploit green corridors, and adjust their behavior to human schedules — often shifting to nocturnal activity in denser areas.

A feeding strategy in which an animal takes advantage of whatever food or water source is available rather than specializing. In urban coyotes, this manifests as highly varied diets and willingness to exploit novel environments — rooftops, parking structures, drainage channels — as resource patches.
